questions.question: Does starting a goroutine guarantee that code runs in parallel?
questions.title: Concurrency is not a parallel-execution guarantee
questions.direct_answer: No. A `go` statement makes a function concurrent, meaning its execution can overlap with other work, but the Go runtime decides when and where it runs. Actual parallel execution requires runnable independent work plus available execution capacity. Correct code must not depend on two goroutines running at the same instant or in a particular order.

interviewer_intent.testing: A practical understanding of runtime-managed concurrency without treating goroutines as magic threads.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming each goroutine owns an OS thread or that lightweight means unlimited and race-free.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the runtime-to-thread relationship while keeping implementation details separate from language guarantees.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A `go` statement creates concurrency, not guaranteed simultaneous execution.
The runtime schedules ready goroutines onto available execution resources.
Blocked or waiting goroutines are not using a processor for Go code at that moment.
Independent CPU work may run in parallel when capacity is available.
Use synchronization for ordering; never rely on which goroutine happens to run first.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Starting a goroutine guarantees an independent concurrent flow, not that two instructions execute at the same physical instant. The new goroutine becomes something the Go runtime may schedule. The caller continues without waiting, and either goroutine may make progress first.

Parallelism happens only when there is more than one runnable piece of work and execution capacity is available. The runtime maps goroutines onto operating-system threads, while `GOMAXPROCS` controls how many processors may execute Go code simultaneously. A goroutine waiting on a channel or supported network operation is not runnable work for a CPU at that moment.

For example, four goroutines can calculate independent squares and send results. The calculations may overlap and results may arrive in any order. Sorting before display makes the required output deterministic without pretending the schedule itself is deterministic.

I use goroutines to structure independent work and synchronization to state the ordering the program requires. If correctness depends on one goroutine running first, I add a channel, mutex, WaitGroup, or another explicit relation. Concurrency can improve utilization, but it is not itself proof of speedup or parallel execution.

sections.title: Ready work and available capacity meet at runtime
sections.content:
Concurrency describes a program with several independent activities. Parallelism describes multiple activities executing simultaneously. A single execution resource can still interleave concurrent goroutines, and a hundred goroutines do not create a hundred processors. Some may be ready, while others wait for channels, timers, locks, or I/O.

The runtime is free to choose a legal schedule, and that schedule changes with load and environment. Tests that pass because one goroutine usually wins are therefore fragile. A channel transfer or lock creates a required order; a scheduler observation does not. Performance decisions need measurement because coordination overhead and resource contention can outweigh any parallel work.

sections.title: What concurrency does and does not promise
sections.content:
| Condition | What can happen | What is not guaranteed |
|---|---|---|
| One new goroutine | Caller and task are concurrent | Task runs first |
| Several runnable CPU tasks | Runtime may execute them in parallel | A speedup |
| Task blocked on channel or I/O | Other ready work may run | Blocked task completes soon |
| Shared mutable state | Accesses may interleave | Race safety |
| Explicit synchronization | Required operations gain an order | A fixed global schedule |

questions.question: When does a goroutine help, and when should the code stay sequential?
questions.title: Choosing concurrent or sequential execution
questions.direct_answer: Use goroutines when independent work can overlap and the benefit justifies coordination—for example, waiting on unrelated network calls or processing independent jobs with a bounded worker count. Keep code sequential when work is tiny, ordered, dependent, or already fast enough. Concurrency adds cancellation, error, ownership, and testing costs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether concurrency is chosen from workload shape rather than as a default optimization.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Starting one goroutine per item without measuring work or limiting external resources.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish overlapping I/O from CPU parallelism and mention bounded concurrency.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Concurrency helps when independent operations can make progress during each other's waits.
CPU work benefits only when tasks are divisible and processing capacity is available.
Sequential code is often clearer for tiny, ordered, or dependent steps.
Bound concurrency to match databases, APIs, memory, and CPU—not the number of inputs.
Measure end-to-end behaviour and include cancellation and error handling in the cost.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I use a goroutine when there is genuinely independent work that can overlap. A common example is fetching three unrelated services: while one request waits on the network, another can progress. For CPU-heavy tasks, concurrency can help only when the algorithm splits cleanly and the runtime has processing capacity to execute parts in parallel.

I keep work sequential when each operation is very small, later steps depend on earlier ones, output order is central, or the measured latency already meets the requirement. Starting and coordinating goroutines adds scheduling, communication, cancellation, and error-collection work. That overhead can make a tiny loop slower and certainly makes it harder to reason about.

I also bound concurrency. For example, importing 100,000 records should not automatically start 100,000 database calls. A fixed worker pool or semaphore can match the database connection limit and apply backpressure.

My boundary is operational rather than stylistic: concurrency must have an owner, a stop condition, and a measurable benefit. If I cannot describe how results, errors, and cancellation return to the caller, the sequential version is the safer design.

sections.title: Find independent waiting, then set a budget
sections.content:
Concurrency changes the shape of waiting. It is valuable when one task would otherwise leave usable resources idle while another independent task could proceed. It does not shorten a dependency chain where step B requires step A's result. Nor does it promise parallel execution; concurrency is structure, while parallelism depends on runtime and hardware.

After finding independent work, choose a budget. External systems often have stricter limits than Go itself: a service rate limit, database connection pool, memory cap, or CPU quota. A bounded number of workers makes that limit visible and prevents a burst of input from becoming an uncontrolled burst of goroutines.

sections.title: Concurrency decision
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Several pieces of work] --> B{Independent?}
  B -- No --> S[Keep sequential]
  B -- Yes --> C{Meaningful I/O wait or divisible CPU work?}
  C -- No --> S
  C -- Yes --> D[Choose a resource limit]
  D --> E[Define results, errors, cancellation]
  E --> F[Measure against sequential baseline]
```
